messages.subject: Spatial LVMs and MVNORM
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I am relatively new to TMB, and have been trying to fit generalized linear latent variable models but am encountering issues trying to put a spatial covariance on the latent variables. As an example, I tried to run the compile tmbmod_spatialLVM.cpp script, and then run TMB on with some example testdata.RData using the following R script:

rm(list = ls())
library(TMB)
compile("tmbmod_spatialLVM.cpp")
dyn.load(dynlib("tmbmod_spatialLVM"))

load(file = "testdata.RData")
p <- ncol(dat$y)
n <- nrow(dat$y)
num.X <- ncol(dat$X)

## Declare parameters
parameters <- list(betas = matrix(runif(p*num.X),p,num.X), loadings = runif(sum(lower.tri(dat$loadings,diag=TRUE))), u = matrix(0, n, dat$num.lv <http://num.lv>))
parameters$covlnphi <- log(1)

## Declare data
data <- list(y = dat$y, x = dat$X, num_lv = dat$num.lv <http://num.lv>, D = pairwise.dist)

whatis.random <- c("u")
objs <- MakeADFun(data, parameters, random = whatis.random, DLL = "tmbmod_spatialLVM")
## For dealing with diagonals on loading matrix
lowerlim <- rep(-Inf, length(objs$par))
lowerlim[p*num.X + which(dat$loadings == diag(dat$loadings))] <- 0

fit <- optim(par = objs$par, fn = objs$fn, gr = objs$gr, method = "L-BFGS-B", lower = lowerlim, hessian = TRUE) ## Cannot optimize!

The above runs into an error as it cannot (even) evaluate the negative complete log-likelihood at the initial parameters. The problem seems to be associated with the way I have coded up the multivariate normal distribution of the latent variables, but I have not been able to fix it. Am I missing something really obvious?

Any advice would be greatly appreciated.

Thanks heaps.

Regards,
Francis

messages.body_plain:
Your loop

 matrix<Type> cov(n,n);
     for (int i=0; i<n; i++) { for (int j=0; j<i; j++) {
          cov(i,j) = exp(-D(i,j)/exp(covlnphi));
          cov(j,i) = cov(i,j);
          } }

doesn't fill the diagonal of cov.
Try 'j<=i' instead.

messages.subject: betabinomial, numerical issues
messages.body_plain:
Playing around with a model involving some seemingly large random effects (of mother id) influencing some small binomial counts (fledling survival) I could not get a particular model alternative to converge.  Including several other random effects of different year etc. works fine, however, presumably because the likelihood contribution for each level of these random effects are much better approximated by the Laplace approximation.  So it seems that these convergence problems may be related to how well the Laplace approximation works for these random effects?

To solve the problem one idea would be to instead use the betabinomial distribution to model overdispersion in the fledgling survival data without having to include any random effect.

This seems to work but only after adding two numerical hacks to the code:

1) If the probabilitiy p predicted by the model is numerically equal to zero or 1 (which easily happen with bad staring values), either alpha and beta of the betabinomial will be numerically equal to zero which causes an error when computing lgamma(alpha) and lgamma(beta).  To solve the problem I simply add 1e-100 to the alpha and beta when computing these.

2) Similarly, in the limit of alpha and beta large such that the betabinomial tends to an ordinary binomial distribution, this too can cause problems because lgamma(alpha + x) and lgamma(alpha) might evaluate to the same value numerically if alpha is greater than about 1e+16.  The likelihood contribution then evaluates to a wrong and same value for all values of the binomial count x). This is a real issue because the optimizer ends up in this limit if there happen to be underdispersion in the data.  To solve this problem I parameterize in terms of the disperion parameter gamma = (alpha + beta + n)/(alpha + beta + 1) and constrain this to be larger than 1+1e-10.

So I guess my question is if there is any better way of doing this or if anyone sees any problems with my current solution?

The code of a toy implementation is at https://github.com/jtufto/tmb-betabinomial.git

messages.subject: Re: [TMB users] betabinomial, numerical issues
messages.body_plain:
I think these hacks are reasonable. If I were incorporating this into a long-term code base I would try to see if there were more numerically stable expressions one could use.  Without thinking about it too carefully, I think in case (1) you do have to clamp but in case (2) you may be able to do better.  For example, in a recent project I used this for negative binomial in a case where the shape parameter could get large.

NBconst <- function(k,x) {
    return(ifelse(x==0,0,-lbeta(k,x)-log(x)))
}
LL ~ NBconst(ll.k,X) +
                       ll.k*(-log1p(mu/ll.k)) +
                       X * log(mu) - X * log(ll.k + mu)

Another tricky thing is that the derivatives of lbeta aren't necessarily numerically stable for large shape parameters, depending on how they're defined.

messages.subject: HMM model for capture-recapture data
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I'm trying to implement a HMM (aka multievent) model in TMB to analyse capture-recapture data. I'm curious about the performance of TMB compared to Rcpp with which I have already implemented the same model (https://github.com/oliviergimenez/multieventRcpp).

With TMB, I run into compilation errors that I do not seem able to sort out :-( I suspect these errors are related to the way I use indexing by a data vector, and also how I handle element-wise vector multiplications.

The code and data are available from https://github.com/oliviergimenez/hmm_tmb. Any help would be much appreciated.

Cheers,
Olivier

messages.subject_clean: [TMB users] HMM model for capture-recapture data
messages.body_plain:
Hi Olivier,

I’m happy to see that you’re interested in this and I’m curious about the benchmarking results. I’d really like to see a few models with discrete latent state variables translated into TMB. I was recently working on converting the lady slipper example from Ch 9 of "Bayesian Population Analysis using WinBUGS --- A Hierarchical Perspective" (2012) by Marc Kéry and Michael Schaub. A goal of this exercise would be to compare some the MCMC methods for TMB to those of STAN and WinBUGS.

I’m almost done with the ladyslipper example, and welcome other people to try others from this chapter. Conveniently, the algorithm for calculating the likelihood while integrating over the discrete latent variables is in these stan examples
https://github.com/stan-dev/example-models/tree/master/BPA

I hope my pull request on GitHub solves the compilation errors. It might be computationally more efficient to replace this
- ALPHA = (ALPHA * A) * B.row(evennt(j)); // vector matrix product, then element-wise vector product

with some linear algebra and typecasting, but I was lazy and didn’t think about it very hard. I didn’t try making ALPHA a matrix, but that could be a solution.

cheers,
Mollie

———————————
Mollie E. Brooks, Ph.D.
Postdoctoral Researcher
National Institute of Aquatic Resources
Technical University of Denmark
